meta.title: Myasthenia Gravis with Myasthenic Crisis
meta.summary: 29F, previously healthy, with 4 days of worsening dyspnoea on a background of 3 months of fatigable proximal weakness, ptosis, diplopia and dysphagia. Recently treated for a UTI with ciprofloxacin. Presents in respiratory distress from new-onset myasthenia gravis precipitating a myasthenic crisis, requiring recognition of neuromuscular respiratory failure and elective intubation.
meta.author: Bader Ali

objectives.overall_goal: Appreciate that patients with myasthenia gravis often present with a crisis, usually preceded by infection or surgery.
medical: Recognise the indications for intubation in patients presenting with respiratory distress who are known for, or have symptoms suggestive of, myasthenia gravis.
Know how to assess respiratory function in neuromuscular disease, where evaluation differs from respiratory distress due to primary pulmonary illness.
Revise the immediate recommended management for myasthenic crisis.
nursing: Recognise the need for early and continuous monitoring of vitals and respiratory status.
Know which signs are most important to follow and how they differ from monitoring of pulmonary-induced respiratory distress.

patient.name: EK
patient.persona: 29-year-old woman, previously healthy, frightened and breathless. Speaks in short fragments and pauses to breathe between words; cannot finish a full sentence in one breath. Sitting upright, refuses to lie flat because it worsens her dyspnoea. Volunteers little unless asked. If asked about symptoms: 3 months of getting weaker, especially by the end of the day; trouble climbing stairs and holding her arms up; trouble chewing (especially steak) and, more recently, swallowing; drooping eyelids and double vision at night. Worse at the end of the day, better in the morning. Will cough and choke if given anything to drink.

presentation.opening_vignette: 29F just arrived to the hospital via EMS due to breathing difficulty and orthopnoea. Previously healthy. On 6 L face mask, sating 97%. Stays in a sitting position, refusing to lie down because of increased dyspnoea.
triage_note: Complains of shortness of breath over several days. Worsening. No chest pain.

history.label: EMS handover
history.content: Called 20 minutes ago for difficulty breathing. On arrival the patient was sitting in a tripod position, tachypnoeic and unable to complete full sentences. O2 sat on scene 96% on room air; oxygen given for comfort. BP and HR otherwise normal. Husband is following by car, ~5 minutes behind.

history.label: Symptoms (from patient)
history.content: 4 days of worsening shortness of breath; worse at night, now sleeping on 3 pillows. Over 3 months, increasing difficulty climbing stairs and holding her arms up, worse at the end of the day. Difficulty chewing (especially steak) at suppertime; more recently difficulty swallowing. For 2 weeks, eyelids drop and she gets double vision when reading before bed.

history.label: Collateral history (husband)
history.content: 3-month history of weakness: initially trouble with the 3 flights of stairs to their apartment (now the third flight is impossible), then arm weakness (cannot style her hair, could not finish painting the apartment because her arms tired). Now dysphagia, most noticeable at end of day. Clear diurnal fluctuation, worse by evening. Left eyelid drooping, better in the morning. Recently treated for a UTI with ciprofloxacin at a walk-in clinic. Non-smoker, occasional alcohol. No headache, LOC, trauma, fever, chills, night sweats or weight loss.

history.label: Family history hint (husband)
history.content: The husband recalls that the patient's mother had some kind of neuromuscular condition, though he cannot remember its name.

findings: Bilateral moderate weakness of CN VII (facial)
Dysarthria that fatigues and worsens during the exam
No nystagmus; no tongue atrophy or palatal deviation
Upper limbs: power preserved but fatigues with repetition; reflexes equal, sensation intact
Lower limbs: power preserved; reflexes equal, sensation intact
No muscle atrophy in any limb
exam.note: Weakness is fatigable — strength declines the longer a movement is repeated. Patient cannot complete a full sentence in one breath.
Pattern is rapid and shallow from respiratory-muscle fatigue, not airway obstruction or consolidation.

findings: S1 + S2 present, no added sounds
Soft and lax; no tenderness, guarding or rebound
Airway clear, no secretions, no swelling or goitre, no trauma
Will cough and choke if given anything to drink (bulbar weakness / unsafe swallow)
exam.note: Bedside swallow demonstrates an unprotected airway — a key indication for intubation in this case.

actors.voice: Breathless, frightened, short fragmented phrases with pauses to breathe.
actors.persona: See patient.persona. Answers only what is asked; symptoms fluctuate and are worse at end of day.

script: We were called 20 minutes ago for difficulty breathing. She was sitting tripod, tachypnoeic, couldn't finish sentences. O2 sat on scene was 96% on room air so we put her on oxygen for comfort. BP and HR are otherwise normal. Her husband is right behind us by car.

actors.voice: Concerned, anxious; wants to know what is going on.
actors.persona: Arrives ~5 minutes after the patient. Does not speak until asked to give history.
script: Gives the 3-month collateral history when asked (see history.husband_collateral).
If learners seem unsure of the cause, volunteers that her mother had some neuromuscular condition he can't name (see history.husband_family_history).

actors.persona: Bedside nurse who can prompt the team.
script: If no collateral history is taken, prompts the team to speak with the husband.
Confirms the neuromuscular-blocker dose before administration.

actors.persona: Assists with bedside respiratory measurements and intubation.
script: Reports vital capacity and negative inspiratory force when asked.
If not already done, prompts plasma exchange and corticosteroids.
Notes that pyridostigmine is NOT used in myasthenic crisis.
If called early, says they will come in 20 minutes — keep working the case meanwhile.
If the team is stuck, calls back and accepts the patient to ICU with myasthenia gravis as the working diagnosis.

investigations.name: Venous blood gas
investigations.result: VBG: pH 7.31, pCO2 55 mmHg, HCO3 26 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L. (Venous sample — use pulse oximetry for oxygenation; pCO2 and pH are reliable.)
investigations.interpretation: Hypercapnic (type-2) respiratory failure from neuromuscular fatigue. The elevated pCO2 and low-normal pH confirm ventilatory failure.

investigations.name: CBC, electrolytes, renal function
investigations.result: CBC, electrolytes, urea/creatinine all within normal limits. No leukocytosis.

investigations.name: ECG
investigations.result: 12-lead ECG recorded; the tracing is up on the monitor for you to read.
investigations.interpretation: Sinus tachycardia ~105 bpm, no ischaemic changes, normal intervals — the rate reflects distress, not a primary cardiac cause.

investigations.name: Chest X-ray
investigations.result: Portable chest film is on the screen for you to review.
investigations.interpretation: No acute consolidation, effusion or pneumothorax; possible subtle anterior mediastinal fullness.
investigations.visual_dx: normal chest, no acute cardiopulmonary process

investigations.name: Bedside vital capacity (VC)
investigations.result: VC less than 20 mL/kg, and falling.
investigations.interpretation: Below the threshold that mandates intubation in neuromuscular respiratory failure.

investigations.name: Negative inspiratory force (NIF)
investigations.interpretation: Markedly weak inspiratory effort — impending respiratory failure.

investigations.name: CT chest (with contrast)
investigations.result: Anterior mediastinal soft-tissue mass measuring 5 x 3 x 3.6 cm. (MRN 5854769).
investigations.interpretation: Suggestive of thymoma — the underlying driver of the myasthenic crisis.

states.name: Baseline — undifferentiated respiratory distress
states.patient_status: Awake, tachypnoeic with shallow breathing. On an oxygen mask. Unable to complete full sentences.
expected_actions: Obtain collateral history from the husband
ECG, CXR and labs including a blood gas

modifiers.description: Respiratory muscles begin to tire: rate climbs and oxygenation slips despite supplemental O2.
Continued respiratory fatigue: SpO2 falling on high-flow O2, accessory muscle use visible.

cues.text: If no collateral history is taken, the nurse prompts the team to speak with the husband.

transitions.description: Completes a focused assessment and recognises a neuromuscular pattern of respiratory failure (collateral history + neuro exam pointing to myasthenia gravis).
transitions.patient_effect: Picture consolidates: fatigable weakness with bulbar and respiratory involvement.

transitions.description: Time passes without the picture being pieced together.

states.facilitator_notes: Learners should focus on a quick primary and secondary assessment. Collateral history from the husband should point toward a neurogenic cause of respiratory failure, with myasthenia gravis most probable.

states.name: Recognition — neuromuscular respiratory failure
states.patient_status: Awake, tachypnoeic with shallow breathing. On an oxygen mask. Unable to complete full sentences. First VBG results are back.
expected_actions: Recognise respiratory status is due to respiratory-muscle fatigue, not a primary lung problem
Note the unprotected airway (coughs/chokes on drinking) and neck flexion < 3/5
Decide on elective intubation and mechanical ventilation

modifiers.description: If intubation is delayed, the patient becomes more distressed and hypoxic as the respiratory muscles fail.

cues.text: The team seems stuck on the diagnosis. Prompt the resident to speak with the husband — he's arrived and is waiting at the bedside, but hasn't been asked anything yet.

transitions.description: Opts for elective intubation and prepares the team for a controlled airway.
transitions.patient_effect: Team moves to a controlled, elective intubation.

states.facilitator_notes: The unsafe swallow and poor neck flexion (a bedside surrogate for respiratory-muscle strength), together with VC < 20 mL/kg, justify elective intubation before frank failure.

states.name: Intubation — paralytic dosing matters
states.patient_status: Awake, tachypnoeic, shallow breathing on oxygen, still unable to complete full sentences. RT reports VC < 20 mL/kg and NIF ~ -25 cmH2O.
expected_actions: Perform a rapid airway assessment and prepare the team for intubation
Account for altered neuromuscular-blocker dosing in myasthenia gravis
Have RT measure vital capacity / NIF

cues.text: The nurse confirms the neuromuscular-blocker dose before administration.

transitions.description: Intubates successfully with appropriate neuromuscular-blocker dosing (resistance to succinylcholine requiring a larger dose; sensitivity to rocuronium requiring a smaller dose).
transitions.patient_effect: Airway secured; patient sedated and ventilated.

transitions.description: Gives a standard dose of succinylcholine: the mouth stays clenched; if forced or if intubation is too slow, the patient gags, vomits and aspirates.
transitions.patient_effect: Failed paralysis and aspiration precipitate decompensation.

states.facilitator_notes: In myasthenia there is relative resistance to succinylcholine (needs larger doses) and relative sensitivity to non-depolarising agents such as rocuronium (needs smaller doses). RT assists with VC/NIF measurement.

states.name: Post-intubation — disposition and crisis management
states.patient_status: Intubated and sedated, ventilated and stable.
expected_actions: Urgent ICU and Neurology consults for admission
Consider plasma exchange or IVIG (confirm dose with Neurology)
Consider and exclude alternative diagnoses (e.g. Guillain-Barré, ALS)

modifiers.description: If ICU is called early, they will come in 20 minutes — the team should keep excluding other conditions and may order further investigations meanwhile.

cues.text: If the team is stuck, ICU calls back and accepts the patient with myasthenia gravis as the working diagnosis.
If not already done, Neurology prompts plasma exchange and corticosteroids, and notes that pyridostigmine is not used in myasthenic crisis.
cues.when: plasma exchange / steroids not yet started

transitions.description: Arranges definitive disposition — ICU admission with crisis therapy (plasma exchange or IVIG) under way.
transitions.patient_effect: Admitted to ICU on plasma exchange/IVIG and steroids.

transitions.description: Time passes after intubation; the patient is accepted to ICU.
transitions.patient_effect: Admitted to ICU on plasma exchange/IVIG and steroids.

transitions.description: Patient accepted to ICU with crisis therapy initiated.
transitions.patient_effect: Admitted to ICU on plasma exchange/IVIG and steroids.

states.facilitator_notes: Recognise that pyridostigmine is NOT used in myasthenic crisis. Immediate management: admit to ICU, monitor respiratory muscle strength, plasma exchange or IVIG, and high-dose glucocorticoids.

states.name: PEA arrest (hypoxic)
expected_actions: Recognise PEA is most likely secondary to hypoxia
Secure the airway and oxygenate; high-quality CPR

transitions.description: Once intubated/oxygenated, after ~2 minutes of CPR the patient achieves ROSC and is moved toward ICU.
transitions.patient_effect: ROSC achieved after correcting hypoxia; patient now intubated and stabilising.

states.facilitator_notes: PEA here is a hypoxic arrest from failed airway management. The reversible cause is hypoxia — oxygenate and ventilate. ROSC follows once the airway is secured.

states.name: Disposition — admitted to ICU
states.patient_status: Intubated, sedated and admitted to ICU with myasthenic crisis treatment under way.

medication_rubric.label: Avoided pyridostigmine
medication_rubric.note: Pyridostigmine is not used in myasthenic crisis.

medication_rubric.label: Chose a non-depolarising paralytic
medication_rubric.note: Prefer a non-depolariser (reversible with sugammadex) over succinylcholine in MG.

medication_rubric.label: Reduced the rocuronium dose
medication_rubric.note: MG patients are markedly sensitive to non-depolarisers — give a smaller dose.

medication_rubric.label: Increased the succinylcholine dose
medication_rubric.note: MG patients are relatively resistant to succinylcholine — a larger dose is needed if it is used.

workup_rubric.label: Examined the neuromuscular system
workup_rubric.note: A focused neuro exam reveals the fatigable weakness, ptosis and neck-flexion weakness central to the diagnosis.

workup_rubric.label: Assessed respiratory status at the bedside
workup_rubric.note: Shallow, fatiguing breathing and a weak cough signal impending neuromuscular respiratory failure.

workup_rubric.label: Measured vital capacity
workup_rubric.note: VC < 15-20 mL/kg is a threshold to intubate in neuromuscular respiratory failure — the single most useful bedside number here.

workup_rubric.label: Measured negative inspiratory force
workup_rubric.note: NIF quantifies inspiratory-muscle strength alongside VC and trends the decline.

workup_rubric.label: Checked a blood gas
workup_rubric.note: A rising pCO2 confirms type-2 (ventilatory) respiratory failure from hypoventilation — do not be reassured by the SpO2.

workup_rubric.label: Imaged the mediastinum for a thymoma
workup_rubric.note: An anterior mediastinal mass (thymoma) is a treatable driver of myasthenia and should be sought.

debrief.summary: Myasthenic crisis is a life-threatening exacerbation of myasthenia gravis defined as worsening myasthenic weakness requiring intubation or non-invasive ventilation. In ~20% of patients presenting in crisis, it is the first manifestation of myasthenia gravis. This patient's crisis was likely precipitated by infection and by ciprofloxacin.
teaching_points: Assess respiratory function in neuromuscular disease with bedside measures (vital capacity, NIF, neck flexion, single-breath count, swallow/secretions) rather than relying on SpO2 — desaturation is a late sign.
Intubate electively when respiratory-muscle strength is failing (e.g. VC < 20-30 mL/kg, weak cough, unsafe swallow) rather than waiting for arrest.

Neuromuscular blockers in MG: relative RESISTANCE to depolarising agents (succinylcholine — needs larger doses) and marked SENSITIVITY to non-depolarising agents (rocuronium/vecuronium — needs smaller doses, reverse with sugammadex).
Immediate crisis management: ICU admission, frequent monitoring of respiratory muscle strength, plasma exchange OR IVIG (400 mg/kg/day x5 days), and high-dose glucocorticoids.
Pyridostigmine is NOT used in myasthenic crisis.
Look for a precipitant (infection, surgery) and for an offending drug.
common_errors: Treating the picture as a primary pulmonary problem and missing the neuromuscular cause.
Relying on SpO2 and delaying intubation until frank respiratory failure or arrest.
Giving a standard dose of succinylcholine and failing to account for altered NMBA dynamics in MG.

discussion.question: What special precautions apply to neuromuscular blockers in myasthenia gravis?
discussion.answer: Use caution with NMBAs. Patients are resistant to depolarising agents (succinylcholine — larger doses) and very sensitive to non-depolarising agents (rocuronium, vecuronium, cisatracurium — small doses, prolonged effect). If an NMBA is needed, prefer rocuronium/vecuronium and reverse with sugammadex.

discussion.question: Other than myasthenia gravis, what can present with similar neuromuscular respiratory failure?
discussion.answer: The most common other causes of acute neuromuscular respiratory failure are Guillain-Barré syndrome and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

discussion.question: Which medications can unmask or worsen myasthenia gravis?
discussion.answer: Antibiotics (aminoglycosides such as gentamicin; fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin; macrolides such as azithromycin/erythromycin), beta-blockers, procainamide, magnesium, chloroquine, gabapentin, phenytoin, lithium, and corticosteroids (can transiently worsen before they help).
